newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania aluminium sector fears energy price hike.
newsitem.headline: Romania aluminium sector fears energy price hike.

text.p: Romania's energy-guzzling aluminium sector says it could be damaged by the plans of the Renel RA utility to raise electricity prices to compensate for the continuous depreciation of the leu currency.

"Aluminium production is vital for this country," a senior official from the ALRO SA aluminium smelter said on Thursday. "Any attempt to obstruct this sector is absurd and against logic," he said by telephone from Slatina.
The official referred to a meeting between Renel and local aluminium producers on Wednesday, during which he said Renel had suggested it might raise the electricity price to $50 per 1.0 MW from $30.
Renel officials were not available for comment.
Such a move could seriously hit ALRO's output and greatly affect its exports, the ALRO official said.
Renel said the price rise was required to cover losses due to the slide of the leu since July 1996, when it last adjusted prices, the official added.
The power utility claims losses of some 900 billion lei since last July because of the leu's depreciation.
Last year, the smelter in Slatina, 200 km west of Bucharest, produced some 140,000 tonnes of aluminium as well as alloys. Of this, some 70 percent was exported.
"We agree that electricity prices should be aligned to the leu's value. But the government should grant subsidies to this sector where electricity is a raw material," the official said.
"We simply want to be treated like aluminium producers in other countries, who enjoy support from the state," he added.

An executive of Conef SA, which groups Romania's state-run non-ferrous smelters, said the holding was considering plans to import electricity from Russia or neighbouring Serbia if Renel jacked up its tariffs.
"There won't be any technical problems," he said. "But to make things easier, the government should keep its promises to break Renel's monopoly."
The Conef executive also said the holding would ask the government to abandon state-controlled prices for aluminium sold on the local market and to align them to world prices.
"It's neither a profit nor an incentive for us to get $900 per tonne of aluminium sold here, when we could get some $1,570 or more for that tonne abroad," he said.
The Slatina smelter, which produces electrolytic and refined aluminium as well as alloys, was recently upgraded to cut energy and material consumption.
The plant upgraded a 25,000-tonne production unit which it plans to open soon to boost output.
